claim: Spiking, IPSCs, and EPSCs were recorded from the soma of an ON-OFF DSGC in response to a positive contrast spot (200 µm diameter; 500 µm/s) moving in the DSGC's preferred (PD) or null direction (ND).
source: Spiking, IPSCs, and EPSCs recorded from the soma of an ON-OFF DSGC in response to a positive contrast spot (200 µm diameter; 500 µm/s) moving in the DSGC's preferred (PD) or null direction (ND).
evidence: Figure 1A shows experimental recordings of spiking, IPSCs, and EPSCs from a DSGC in response to moving spots.

claim: The orientations of SAC dendrites can predict the PD of DSGCs, because SACs release GABA maximally for stimuli moving from their soma towards their dendritic tips.
source: The orientations of SAC dendrites can predict the PD of DSGCs, because SACs release GABA maximally for stimuli moving from their soma towards their dendritic tips.
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 1C caption and is based on established knowledge about SAC function.

claim: The known anatomy predicts variable and sometimes disorganized local tuning in DSGCs.
source: The known anatomy predicts variable and sometimes disorganized local tuning in DSGCs (blue region).
evidence: This is inferred from the anatomical reconstruction shown in Figure 1C and discussed in the text.

claim: Inhibition shapes direction selectivity independently within small dendritic segments (<10µm) with remarkable accuracy.
source: We demonstrate that inhibition shapes direction selectivity independently within small dendritic segments (<10µm) with remarkable accuracy.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: The parallel processing schemes proposed for direction encoding could be more fine-grained than previously envisioned.
source: The data suggest that the parallel processing schemes proposed for direction encoding could be more fine-grained than previously envisioned.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings presented in the study.

claim: Direction-selective ganglion cells (DSGCs) fire action potentials in response to objects moving in their preferred direction but not in the null direction.
source: objects in the visual scene that move over a DSGC's receptive field in its 'preferred' direction drive excitation onto its dendrites that trigger action potential firing, but for motion in the opposite or 'null' direction, excitation is 'vetoed' by coincident GABAergic inhibition
evidence: This is a well-established property of DSGCs described in the introduction and supported by Figure 1.

claim: Direction-selective GABAergic signals in DSGCs arise from the distal varicosities located on the radiating dendrites of presynaptic starburst amacrine cells (SACs).
source: It is well-established that direction-selective (DS) GABAergic signals in DSGCs arise from the distal varicosities located on the radiating dendrites of presynaptic starburst amacrine cells (SACs; Taylor and Smith, 2012; Vaney et al., 2012; Wei, 2018).
evidence: This is stated as well-established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: SAC varicosities are more effectively depolarized during centrifugal motion (from the soma to the dendritic tip).
source: SAC varicosities are more effectively depolarized during centrifugal motion (from the soma to the dendritic tip), and thus the orientation of a given SAC dendrite provides an approximation of its preferred direction (Euler et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation to Euler et al., 2002.

claim: SAC dendrites with similar orientations tend to make synapses with the same type of DSGC.
source: In a seminal study combining physiological recordings with serial block-face electron microscopy, Briggman et al. (2011) demonstrated that SAC dendrites with similar orientations—and therefore similar directional preferences—tend to make synapses with the same type of DSGC (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Briggman et al. (2011) and supported by Figure 1C.

claim: SACs provide symmetrical excitatory cholinergic signals to DSGCs, which appear to be mediated by a diffuse synaptic mechanism that makes them insensitive to specific wiring patterns.
source: It should be noted that SACs also provide symmetrical excitatory cholinergic signals to DSGCs, which appear to be mediated by a diffuse synaptic mechanism that makes them insensitive to specific wiring patterns (Briggman et al., 2011; Brombas et al., 2017; Lee et al., 2010; Sethuramanujam et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with multiple supporting citations.

claim: The spatial offsets in the GABAergic and cholinergic connectivity produce E/I timing differences that contribute to the overall tuning properties of DSGCs.
source: The resulting spatial offsets in the GABAergic and cholinergic connectivity produce E/I timing differences that contribute to the overall tuning properties of DSGCs (Hanson et al., 2019; Koch et al., 1982; Taylor et al., 2000; Torre and Poggio, 1978).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: A closer inspection of the orientation of presynaptic SACs shows that their dendritic orientation can change systematically throughout a DSGC's dendritic field and can be disorganized in particular dendritic subfields.
source: A closer inspection of the orientation of presynaptic SACs shows that their dendritic orientation can change systematically throughout a DSGC's dendritic field and can be disorganized in particular dendritic subfields (Figure 1C; see dendrites highlighted in blue).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: The anatomy predicts that the inhibitory input to DSGCs will be heterogeneous, and result in frequent inaccuracies in local tuning in dendrites.
source: Thus, the anatomy predicts that the inhibitory input to DSGCs will be heterogeneous, and result in frequent inaccuracies in local tuning in dendrites.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the anatomical observations described in the text.

claim: There is significant variance in the directional tuning of individual SAC varicosities with similar dendritic orientations.
source: Second, Ca2+ imaging studies suggest that there is significant variance in the directional tuning of individual SAC varicosities with similar dendritic orientations (Morrie and Feller, 2018), which is exacerbated by large trial-to-trial variability (Ding et al., 2016; Poleg-Polsky et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations to Ca2+ imaging studies.

claim: DSGCs fire TTX-sensitive dendritic spikes that are directionally tuned.
source: Similar to reports in ON-OFF DSGCs (Oesch et al., 2005; Trenholm et al., 2014), this study directly demonstrated that DSGCs fire TTX-sensitive dendritic spikes that are directionally tuned.
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations to previous studies.

claim: Dendritic spike initiation is driven by localized excitatory activity, and dendritic spike suppression requires inhibition to act in close proximity to the site of excitatory input.
source: Critically, their data suggest that dendritic spike initiation is driven by localized excitatory activity, and that dendritic spike suppression requires inhibition to act in close proximity to the site of excitatory input (Sivyer and Williams, 2013).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Sivyer and Williams, 2013.

claim: DSGCs integrate information over 'subunits' (up to 50–100 µm diameter) that are electrically isolated from each other but relatively isopotential within.
source: Previous modeling estimates based on the natural branching patterns and theoretical voltage length constants of ganglion cell dendrites support the idea that DSGCs integrate information over 'subunits' (up to 50–100 µm diameter) that are electrically isolated from each other but relatively isopotential within (Koch et al., 1982; Schachter et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations to modeling studies.

claim: With NaV blocked, the dendritic Ca2+ signals arise from Ca2+ influx through both voltage-gated Ca2+ channels (CaV) and NMDA receptors.
source: With NaV blocked, the dendritic Ca2+ signals arise from Ca2+ influx through both voltage-gated Ca2+ channels (CaV) and NMDA receptors (Poleg-Polsky and Diamond, 2016; Sethuramanujam et al., 2017), which we provide evidence for in several subsequent experiments (Figures 2–3 and 6).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations and references to experimental evidence in the manuscript.

claim: Ca2+ signals were first observed at dendritic regions of interest (ROIs) located closest to where the moving stimulus entered the DSGC's receptive field.
source: Ca2+ signals were first observed at dendritic regions of interest (ROIs) located closest to where the moving stimulus entered the DSGC's receptive field. Sites positioned later in the stimulus trajectory had progressively delayed response onsets (Figure 2A–D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2A-D.

claim: Using the response latency and relative position of the dendritic sites, the stimulus speed was estimated to be 524 ± 28 µm/s (n = 6), close to the nominal stimulus speed (500 µm/s).
source: Using the response latency and relative position of the dendritic sites, the stimulus speed was estimated to be 524 ± 28 µm/s (n = 6), close to the nominal stimulus speed (500 µm/s; Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement reported in the text and shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The sequential activation of dendrites was also observed when NMDA receptors were blocked (50 µM D-AP5).
source: The sequential activation of dendrites was also observed when NMDA receptors were blocked (50 µM D-AP5).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation.

claim: Individual dendritic branches are depolarized in sequence as the stimulus crosses the DSGC's receptive field.
source: This helped decrease fluctuations in signal amplitude that arise from the asynchronous arrival times of single photons during the one microsecond dwell time at each image pixel, thereby improving signal to noise at low light levels characteristic of sparse synaptic activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the sequential activation of Ca2+ responses observed in the experiments.

claim: The dendritic arbor is not acting as a single unit, but rather individual dendritic branches process their synaptic inputs independently.
source: The data suggest that the dendritic arbor is not acting as a single unit, but rather that individual dendritic branches process their synaptic inputs independently.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations of sequential dendritic activation.

claim: Ca2+ signals evoked by null stimuli were significantly weaker or absent in the majority of sites throughout the dendritic tree.
source: We found that Ca2+ signals evoked by null stimuli were significantly weaker or absent in the majority of sites throughout the dendritic tree (Figure 2F–G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2F-G.

claim: The lack of Ca2+ signals during null motion indicates the presence of strong and coincident inhibition at each dendrite.
source: Since the overall strength of excitation is similar to that evoked by motion in the preferred direction (Park et al., 2014; Yonehara et al., 2013; Hanson et al., 2019), the lack of Ca2+ signals indicates the presence of strong and coincident inhibition at each dendrite.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observations, supported by citations.

claim: Isolated dendritic 'hot spots' (FWHM = 3.0 ± 1.2 µm; n = 61 sites in 7 cells) were occasionally observed during null motion.
source: However, we did occasionally observe activity in isolated dendritic 'hot spots' (FWHM = 3.0 ± 1.2 µm; n = 61 sites in 7 cells) during null motion (Figure 2G–I).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement reported in the text and shown in Figure 2G-I.

claim: Ca2+ signals during null motion were not consistently observed over multiple presentations of the null stimulus at any given site, suggesting that they arise from probabilistic transmission rather than from the absence of inhibitory synapses.
source: These Ca2+ signals were not consistently observed over multiple presentations of the null stimulus at any given site, suggesting that they arise from probabilistic transmission rather than from the absence of inhibitory synapses in that local dendritic region (Figure 2H–I).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observations shown in Figure 2H-I.

claim: Highly localized Ca2+ signals, which persist for hundreds of milliseconds, may be indicative of strong buffering mechanisms in dendrites.
source: Such highly compartmentalized Ca2+ signals, which persist for hundreds of milliseconds, may be indicative of strong buffering mechanisms in dendrites (Awatramani et al., 2007; Biess et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed Ca2+ signal properties, with supporting citations.

claim: The peak amplitudes of the Ca2+ responses exhibited considerable trial-to-trial fluctuations in response to orthogonal motion.
source: In this direction, where E/I levels are more comparable, the peak amplitudes of the Ca2+ responses exhibited considerable trial-to-trial fluctuations (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Only nearby ROIs were significantly correlated with each other, and noise correlations measured in neighboring ROIs were absent when trials were shuffled.
source: Only nearby ROIs were significantly correlated with each other, and noise correlations measured in neighboring ROIs were absent when trials were shuffled (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The correlation strength rapidly decayed over distance with a space constant of λ = 5.3 µm (n = 6 cells), suggesting that Ca2+ signals beyond this distance arise independently.
source: The correlation strength rapidly decayed over distance with a space constant of λ = 5.3 µm (Figure 3D–E; n = 6 cells), suggesting that Ca2+ signals beyond this distance arise independently.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement reported in the text and shown in Figure 3D-E, with an inference about independence.

claim: Trial-to-trial variability was significantly lower when Ca2+ signals were evoked by directly depolarizing the DSGC through the patch electrode in the presence of synaptic blockers.
source: First, trial-to-trial variability was significantly lower when Ca2+ signals were evoked by directly depolarizing the DSGC through the patch electrode in the presence of synaptic blockers (50 µM DL-AP4, 20 µM CNQX, 10 µM UBP-310; Figure 3F–G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 3F-G.

claim: The response variability to motion in the PD was significantly less than that of orthogonal motion.
source: Second, the response variability to motion in the PD—in which inhibition is quite low—was significantly less than that of orthogonal motion.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation.

claim: The response variability during orthogonal motion was significantly reduced in mice where GABA release from SACs was selectively disrupted using the conditional deletion of the vesicular GABA transporter (Slc32a1fl/fl::ChatCre; vGAT KO).
source: Third, the response variability during orthogonal motion was significantly reduced in mice where GABA release from SACs was selectively disrupted using the conditional deletion of the vesicular GABA transporter (Slc32a1fl/fl::ChatCre; vGAT KO; Pei et al., 2015; Figure 3G; Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The response variability is largely synaptic in origin.
source: Nevertheless, these results confirm that the response variability is largely synaptic in origin.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations described in the text.

claim: Ca2+ responses extracted from small dendritic segments (3–4 µm in length) throughout the arbor were well-tuned for the direction of motion.
source: Ca2+ responses extracted from small dendritic segments (3–4 µm in length) throughout the arbor were well-tuned for the direction of motion.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation.

claim: The directional tuning of the somatic spiking was significantly narrower than that of the subthreshold somatic voltage (measured with NaV activity blocked).
source: Indeed, the directional tuning of the somatic spiking was significantly narrower than that of the subthreshold somatic voltage (measured with NaV activity blocked).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation.

claim: The tuning width of the dendritic Ca2+ signals was indistinguishable from that of the spiking response.
source: Interestingly, the tuning width of the dendritic Ca2+ signals was indistinguishable from that of the spiking response (Figure 4A–C), suggesting that the thresholding operations provided by dendritic NaV (Oesch et al., 2005; Sivyer and Williams, 2013; Trenholm et al., 2014) may be similar to those implemented by the nonlinearities associated with Ca2+ influx.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 4A-C, with an inference about the mechanism.

claim: The average PDs of nearby dendritic sites were similar, but they did not necessarily covary over each stimulus set.
source: Although the average PDs of nearby dendritic sites were similar, they did not necessarily covary over each stimulus set (eight directions per set), consistent with the idea that nearby dendritic sites are subject to different sources of synaptic noise.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation with an inference about the underlying mechanism.

claim: The direction encoded by a given site rarely fell in the wrong directional hemisphere, even when computed over a single set of trials (9/353 sites in 7 cells, 2.5%).
source: The direction encoded by a given site rarely fell in the wrong directional hemisphere, even when computed over a single set of trials (9/353 sites in 7 cells, 2.5%).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement reported in the text.

claim: The overall variation in the PD from single stimulus sets (angular standard deviation, σθ = 52.8°; 353 ROIs from 7 cells) was reduced when three to five stimulus sets were averaged (σθ = 31.6°).
source: The overall variation in the PD from single stimulus sets (angular standard deviation, σθ = 52.8°; 353 ROIs from 7 cells) was reduced when three to five stimulus sets were averaged (σθ = 31.6°, Figure 5A,C).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement reported in the text and shown in Figure 5A,C.

claim: The strength of the tuning, quantified using the direction selectivity index (DSI), varied among the population of dendritic sites (DSI = 0.19 ± 0.08; µ ± s.d.; 353 ROIs from 7 cells).
source: In addition, we found that the strength of the tuning, quantified using the direction selectivity index (DSI, ranging from 0 to 1; see Materials and methods), also varied among the population of dendritic sites (DSI = 0.19 ± 0.08; µ ± s.d.; 353 ROIs from 7 cells; Figure 5B,D).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement reported in the text and shown in Figure 5B,D.

claim: Adjacent sites with similar PDs could have large differences in DSI, and vice versa, indicating that the directional tuning of each site arises independently.
source: Interestingly, adjacent sites with similar PDs could have large differences in DSI, and vice versa, indicating that the directional tuning of each site arises independently (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 5E, with an inference about independence.

claim: Sites with a low DSI (<0.1) had significantly weaker Ca2+ responses to preferred motion than those with a high DSI (∆F/F = 0.60 ± 0.09 versus 1.02 ± 0.12, p<0.01, t-test, µ ± s.d.).
source: In response to preferred motion, sites with a low DSI (<0.1) had significantly weaker Ca2+ responses than those with a high DSI (∆F/F = 0.60 ± 0.09 versus 1.02 ± 0.12, p<0.01, t-test, µ ± s.d.).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement with statistical comparison reported in the text.

claim: The null responses at the low DSI sites were generally stronger than those observed at the high DSI sites (∆F/F = 0.49 ± 0.08 versus 0.31 ± 0.05, p<0.01, t-test, µ ± s.d.).
source: However, the null responses at the low DSI sites were generally stronger than those observed at the high DSI sites (∆F/F = 0.49 ± 0.08 versus 0.31 ± 0.05, p<0.01, t-test, µ ± s.d.).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement with statistical comparison reported in the text.

claim: The population of sites with low DSI still computed the correct direction on average, deviating by 0.99 ± 52° from the PD computed from the spiking responses (n = 37 sites in 7 cells, µ ± s.d.).
source: Despite their weak tuning, the population of sites with low DSI still computed the correct direction on average, deviating by 0.99 ± 52° from the PD computed from the spiking responses (n = 37 sites in 7 cells, µ ± s.d.).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement reported in the text.

claim: DS information is highly accurate throughout the dendritic arbor.
source: Together these data suggest that DS information is highly accurate throughout the dendritic arbor.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations described in the text.

claim: Ca2+ responses measured in the presence of the NMDA receptor antagonist D-AP5 (50 µM) were weaker but still well-tuned for direction.
source: Consistent with this notion, we found that Ca2+ responses measured in the presence of the NMDA receptor antagonist D-AP5 (50 µM) were weaker but still well-tuned for direction (Figure 6A–B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 6A-B.

claim: Under NMDA receptor blockade conditions, the distribution of PDs (p=0.49, Angular Distance test; T [0.55]<TC [1.96], Watson-Williams test) and DSIs (p=0.15, Kolmogorov-Smirnov test) throughout the dendritic arbor were indistinguishable from that measured under control conditions.
source: Under these conditions, the distribution of PDs (p=0.49, Angular Distance test; T [0.55]<TC [1.96], Watson-Williams test; Figure 6C) and DSIs (p=0.15, Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, Figure 6D) throughout the dendritic arbor were indistinguishable from that measured under control conditions.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement with statistical tests reported in the text and shown in Figure 6C-D.

claim: NMDA receptors appear to multiplicatively scale dendritic Ca2+ signals.
source: Thus, NMDA receptors appear to multiplicatively scale dendritic Ca2+ signals, making them particularly useful for visualizing E/I interactions in the dendritic tree without disrupting them.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations with NMDA receptor blockade.

claim: Synaptically-evoked Ca2+ signals are expected to be more compartmentalized than dendritic voltage.
source: Synaptically-evoked Ca2+ signals are expected to be more compartmentalized than dendritic voltage (Wybo et al., 2019; Meier and Borst, 2019; Grimes et al., 2010), since they arise from inherently nonlinear sources (voltage-gated Ca2+ channels and NMDA receptors).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations and reasoning about the nonlinear sources.

claim: Dendritic nonlinearities are expected to promote the independence of dendritic activity.
source: Such nonlinearities are also expected to promote the independence of dendritic activity (Grimes et al., 2010), and could explain how nearby dendritic regions could have different directional tuning properties.
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation and an inference about the mechanism.

claim: The model was driven by 177 inhibitory and excitatory inputs each, which integrated to produce somatic currents and spiking responses that were similar to those measured experimentally at the soma.
source: The model was driven by 177 inhibitory and excitatory inputs each, which integrated to produce somatic currents and spiking responses that were similar to those measured experimentally at the soma (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Systematically thresholding the voltage data from −55 mV to −48 mV led to an increase in both the angular variance (σθ = 25.4°, 40.4°, and 45.0° for −55 mV, −50 mV, and −48 mV thresholds, respectively) and the DSI (DSI = 0.42, 0.70, and 0.80 for −55 mV, −50 mV, and −48 mV thresholds, respectively).
source: We found that systematically thresholding the voltage data from −55 mV to −48 mV led to an increase in both the angular variance (σθ = 25.4°, 40.4°, and 45.0° for −55 mV, −50 mV, and −48 mV thresholds, respectively) and the DSI (DSI = 0.42, 0.70, and 0.80 for −55 mV, −50 mV, and −48 mV thresholds, respectively; Figure 7D).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the computational model reported in the text and shown in Figure 7D.

claim: When responses were strongly thresholded, even sites located on neighboring branches encoded different directions, indicating their functional independence.
source: When responses were strongly thresholded, even sites located on neighboring branches encoded different directions, indicating their functional independence (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 7C, with an inference about independence.

claim: The model data support the idea that dendritic nonlinearities could help promote compartmentalized directional tuning in dendrites.
source: The model data support the idea that dendritic nonlinearities could help promote compartmentalized directional tuning in dendrites.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the computational modeling results.

claim: SAC ablation increased the spiking activity in the null direction and thus diminished direction selectivity, likely due to a decrease in inhibition from the ablated SACs.
source: SAC ablation increased the spiking activity in the null direction and thus diminished direction selectivity, likely due to a decrease in inhibition from the ablated SACs (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 8B, with an inference about the mechanism.

claim: After SAC ablation, the directional tuning was highly heterogeneous within imaged regions of the DSGC dendritic arbor.
source: Notably, after SAC ablation we found that the directional tuning was highly heterogeneous within imaged regions of the DSGC dendritic arbor. Many dendritic sites were well-tuned for direction, similar to control conditions, while others were poorly tuned (Figure 8C,E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 8C,E.

claim: The overall DSI distribution after SAC ablation was significantly different than that measured without SAC ablation (p=10−16, Kolmogorov-Smirnov test).
source: The overall DSI distribution was significantly different than that measured without SAC ablation (p=10−16, Kolmogorov-Smirnov test; Figure 8E).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement with statistical test reported in the text and shown in Figure 8E.

claim: The null direction Ca2+ signals at poorly tuned sites were large after SAC ablation.
source: Consistent with the idea that SAC ablation results in a reduction in local inhibition, the null direction Ca2+ signals at poorly tuned sites were large (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Neighboring dendritic sites could have dramatically different DSIs after SAC ablation.
source: Importantly, neighboring dendritic sites could have dramatically different DSIs after SAC ablation (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Sites that were unaffected by SAC ablation were closely interspersed among strongly affected sites, suggesting that the inhibitory inputs to a given site have limited influence on the tuning of its neighbors.
source: Sites that were unaffected by SAC ablation were closely interspersed among strongly affected sites, suggesting that the inhibitory inputs to a given site have limited influence on the tuning of its neighbors (Figure 8F–G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 8F-G, with an inference about the spatial extent of inhibitory influence.

claim: Local inhibitory inputs shape DS Ca2+ responses within single dendritic branches.
source: These data demonstrate that local inhibitory inputs shape DS Ca2+ responses within single dendritic branches.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the SAC ablation experiments.

claim: SAC inhibition is highly directional and can act extremely locally (~5–10 µm scale).
source: One of the central claims of this study is that SAC inhibition is highly directional and can act extremely locally (~5–10 µm scale).
evidence: This is stated as a central claim of the study, supported by the experimental data presented.

claim: Inhibition vetoes local excitatory signals that appear non-directional, resulting in the production of small independent DS dendritic subunits throughout the DGSC's dendritic tree.
source: Inhibition vetoes local excitatory signals that appear non-directional, resulting in the production of small independent DS dendritic subunits throughout the DGSC's dendritic tree (Figures 2–5).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion supported by data in Figures 2-5.

claim: Accurate DS information was present within each subunit even on a single set of trials.
source: Accurate DS information was present within each subunit even on a single set of trials.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation.

claim: There are at most 1–4 SAC synapses within each dendritic subunit.
source: Given that there are at most 1–4 SAC synapses within each dendritic subunit (Bleckert et al., 2013; Jeon et al., 2002; Sigal et al., 2015), it is likely that the output of single SACs are graded according to direction, similar to their Ca2+ responses (Euler et al., 2002; Poleg-Polsky et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations to anatomical studies.

claim: The output of single SACs are likely graded according to direction, similar to their Ca2+ responses.
source: Given that there are at most 1–4 SAC synapses within each dendritic subunit (Bleckert et al., 2013; Jeon et al., 2002; Sigal et al., 2015), it is likely that the output of single SACs are graded according to direction, similar to their Ca2+ responses (Euler et al., 2002; Poleg-Polsky et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observations and cited literature.

claim: Removing inhibition arising from a few SACs on the null side of the receptive field resulted in the loss of direction selectivity in small sections of the dendrite (~10 µm).
source: Support for these hypotheses came from the SAC ablation experiments, where we found that removing inhibition arising from a few SACs on the null side of the receptive field resulted in the loss of direction selectivity in small sections of the dendrite (~10 µm; Figure 8).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 8.

claim: After SAC ablation, robust DS and non-DS sites could be observed on the same dendritic branch, demonstrating the fine spatial scale over which inhibition can veto excitatory responses.
source: After SAC ablation, robust DS and non-DS sites could be observed on the same dendritic branch, demonstrating the fine spatial scale over which inhibition can veto excitatory responses.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation from the SAC ablation experiments.

claim: Inhibition's 'visibility' is expected to be more spatiotemporally constrained compared to excitation because inhibition acts as a shunt.
source: However, since inhibition is thought to act as a shunt, its 'visibility' is expected to be more spatiotemporally constrained compared to excitation (Koch et al., 1982; Rall, 1964; Torre and Poggio, 1978; Williams, 2004), and may have a dominant effect on the local variance.
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations to theoretical work.

claim: SAC varicosities provide reliable, localized, and systematic DS inhibition throughout the entire DSGC dendritic tree.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that SAC varicosities provide reliable, localized, and systematic DS inhibition throughout the entire DSGC dendritic tree.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations presented in the study.

claim: Different dendrites are activated at different times when a stimulus sweeps over the DSGC's receptive field.
source: Although excitatory signals alone may drive depolarizations over larger dendritic areas, it is by no means uniform across the dendritic tree when a stimulus sweeps over the DSGC's receptive field—different dendrites are activated at different times (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The precise timing and placement of each inhibitory input from SACs is critical because mistimed or misplaced E/I are not expected to strongly interact.
source: This makes the precise timing and placement of each inhibitory input from SACs more critical, since mistimed or misplaced E/I are not expected to strongly interact (Hao et al., 2009; Koch et al., 1983; Liu, 2004; Lowe, 2002; Marlin and Carter, 2014; Müller et al., 2012; Müllner et al., 2015; Polsky et al., 2004; Takahashi et al., 2016; Williams, 2004).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations to previous work on E/I interactions.

claim: The presynaptic networks must deliver the 'correct' amount of E/I to each dendrite for each given direction with temporal precision.
source: Thus, the presynaptic networks must deliver the 'correct' amount of E/I to each dendrite for each given direction with temporal precision.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations and theoretical considerations.

claim: In response to null motion, E/I mostly arrive at the same time and place at each point in the dendritic arbor.
source: In response to null motion, we only occasionally observed Ca2+ responses that were localized to small dendritic segments, suggesting that E/I mostly arrive at the same time and place at each point in the dendritic arbor (Figure 2).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observations shown in Figure 2.

claim: Even E/I delays in the range of ~10 ms could significantly compromise the directional spiking output of the DSGCs.
source: While the precise temporal characteristics of E/I cannot be determined by Ca2+ imaging, in a computational model based on the morphology of DSGCs, we found that even E/I delays in the range of ~10 ms could significantly compromise the directional spiking output of the DSGCs (deRosenroll and Awatramani, unpublished data).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from unpublished computational modeling work.

claim: Spatiotemporally coordinated E/I may naturally arise from the co-transmission of GABA and ACh from SAC synapses.
source: It is possible that spatiotemporally coordinated E/I naturally arises from the co-transmission of GABA and ACh from SAC synapses.
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism underlying coordinated E/I.

claim: ACh is released from SACs of all dendritic orientations onto DSGC dendrites, and input from a single SAC is capable of eliciting dendritic spiking.
